query: Earlier studies used carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains unavailable. Prior comparative work produced sharply different outcomes among multimetal nanoparticle systems—including homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high decomposition temperatures—without establishing a general cause. The challenge increases with more than five interacting elements and the requirement to preserve substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications. Against this background, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and why? Describe one controlled comparison without naming the variable or investigative technique, predict the observations relative to an unchanged baseline, define where the hypothesis should and should not apply, relate it to the reported comparative evidence, and identify a decisive falsifying result.

generation.hypothesis: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by the ability to synchronize the reduction kinetics of the different metal precursors. When reaction conditions are tuned to induce near‐simultaneous reduction (thereby synchronizing nucleation events), the resulting nanoparticles form a uniform, solid-solution structure; conversely, when reduction events occur sequentially, the system tends toward phase separation and elemental segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous mixture of precursor compounds for multiple noble and catalytic metals (typically adsorbed/supported on a conductive or absorptive substrate).
generation.intervention: Adjustment of reaction conditions (for example, via a rapid heating method or controlled dropwise addition) to modulate the reduction rate such that the onset and progression of metal reduction occur in synchrony.
generation.conditions: Experimental setups in which one pathway is modified to achieve faster and nearly simultaneous reduction of all metal precursors versus an otherwise identical baseline where the reduction kinetics are not deliberately synchronized.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of uniformly small nuclei clusters throughout the reaction medium, which mediates high-entropy mixing by preventing early-stage elemental segregation.
generation.mechanism: By adjusting the reaction conditions to synchronize the reduction events, the system avoids preferential nucleation from the faster-reducing metal ions that would otherwise dominate the early stages of growth. This synchronization ensures that all metal atoms co-deposit to form a high-entropy alloy before significant diffusion or phase separation can occur.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under synchronized reduction conditions, the nanoparticles will exhibit uniform elemental distribution and a controlled, small particle size. In contrast, the baseline (unsynchronized conditions) will result in phase-separated or core–shell structures with evident elemental segregation.
generation.baseline: A reaction protocol using conventional or unmodified conditions that lead to sequential reduction events, causing nonuniform metal incorporation and phase separation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies primarily to systems where the reduction kinetics are sensitive to external reaction conditions (such as heating rate, dropwise addition, or use of specific additives). It may not apply in cases where large inherent differences in redox potentials dominate or when support effects or solvent interactions overshadow the reduction kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: While existing evidence supports the significance of synchronized reduction, the exact parameters required to achieve this in increasingly complex (more than five elements) systems remain to be precisely determined. Additionally, the influence of various supports or reaction media may introduce complexities not fully addressed in current studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a controlled synthesis of noble metal-based nanoparticles using two reaction protocols with identical precursor compositions. In the first protocol, adjust only the reaction condition that modulates the reduction rate to achieve synchronized reduction (for example, by using rapid heating or carefully timed dropwise addition). In the second (baseline) protocol, use the traditional or unmodified reaction condition that permits sequential reduction. Characterize the resulting nanoparticles with high-resolution elemental mapping (e.g., EDS) and particle size analysis.
measurements: Elemental distribution uniformity (e.g., via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy mapping)
Particle size distribution and morphology (via TEM or STEM)
Phase purity and crystallinity (via XRD or EXAFS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles produced under the synchronized reduction condition do not show a statistically significant improvement in elemental homogeneity and a reduction in phase segregated structures compared to the baseline condition, then the hypothesis that synchronized reduction governs successful HEA nanoparticle formation will be falsified.

Our FMBP strategy allows the metal precursors to rapidly reach 923 K within 5 s (a propulsion speed of 20 cm s−1) with the temperature in the heating zone only dropping to 920 K (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Movie 1). The FMBP strategy ensures the simultaneous pyrolysis of the mixed metal precursors (Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2) due to rapidly reaching the high temperature (above the pyrolysis temperature of all precursors), resulting in the high supersaturation of monomers, in turn forming smaller nuclei clusters to form HEA-NPs without phase separation (Fig. 1b). In contrast, the FBP strategy can only synthesize phase-separated alloy, because each metal precursor would be reduced in sequence for their various reduction potentials during temperature programming (20 K min−1) (Fig. 1b). Moreover, we simulate the heat transfer of 20 mg of precursors/graphene oxide (GO) placed in a quartz boat (the commercial ANSYS FLUENT software). The results showed that GO could reach 923 K within 5 s, which was consistent with the time of the actual experimental operation (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Movie 2).

In our FMBP, the mixed metal precursors could rapidly reach the high temperature (e.g. 923 K). The time for the supports such as GO, zeolite, and γ-Al2O3 supporting precursors to reach 923 K in the FMBP process were simulated. The results revealed that these supports could reach 923 K within 5 s, showing almost no difference with the practical operation (Supplementary Fig. 24 and Movies 1 and 2). It should be noted that all metal precursors with different properties could be efficiently decomposed under 923 K (Supplementary Tables 4–8). Therefore, in the FMBP process (Fig. 5a, c), the formation of HEA-NPs was thermodynamically favored due to the low critical excess free energy (∆Gr*). The nuclei of alloys with the small size will be much favorable due to the fact that these monomers only need little energy for nucleation,. In contrast, in FBP (Fig. 5b) or SMBP, the formation of alloys slowly going through the low temperature (e.g. 673 K) with the slow heating way would result in the larger radius of nuclei, and the phase separation would occur due to the high ∆Gr* (Fig. 4c–f).
